analysis.one_liner: Bans Congress from delegating lawmaking power, invalidating federal rules not written by Congress itself.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2020 with no cosponsors, the bill was sent to committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal law to prohibit Congress from delegating lawmaking power to anyone — agencies, the President, courts, or states. Any new presidential directive, rule, or regulation not fully spelled out in an act of Congress would have no force, and citizens could sue to block enforcement. It would also require the Government Accountability Office to report which existing laws contain such delegations so they could be phased out.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the bill would chiefly benefit businesses subject to federal regulation, which would face far fewer enforceable rules — environmental, workplace, financial, drug and food safety, and consumer protection rules are mostly written by agencies under broad laws passed by Congress. It would also benefit companies and individuals who wanted to challenge federal rules in court, since it creates a new cause of action against the government.

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits any act of Congress from delegating legislative power to any agency, the executive branch, the courts, states, or any other entity [S2].

Any presidential directive, rule, or regulation issued 90 days after enactment that is not authorized by a fully defined act of Congress would have no force or effect, and no legal or regulatory action could be brought under it [S3].
It gives any aggrieved person the right to sue the United States to block enforcement of any law, directive, or regulation that does not comply with the nondelegation requirement [S3].
It requires the Comptroller General to report to Congress within six months on all existing statutes containing prohibited delegations, so those could be phased out [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who relies on federal regulation: workers relying on workplace safety rules, consumers relying on financial and product protections, and communities relying on air, water, and food safety standards. Congress would have to define every rule fully in statute — a task it has never had the capacity to perform for the tens of thousands of technical rules federal law requires — leaving a gap where protections simply stop being issued or updated.
analysis.who_pays_short: Anyone relying on federal regulatory protections

drawbacks.text: Federal agencies cannot function under the bill's standard: modern regulation depends on agencies filling in technical details — safety thresholds, approval processes, compliance deadlines — that Congress could never write into statute itself, so most federal rulemaking would stop [S2].

Existing statutes with delegations would not be automatically voided, but the GAO report contemplates phasing them out, and no new rules could issue even under longstanding laws, creating an immediate enforcement gap in areas from drug safety to environmental limits [S2] [S3].
The new right to sue the federal government over any rule not 'fully and completely defined' in statute would flood the courts with challenges to nearly every federal regulation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill makes a real constitutional argument: elected lawmakers, not unelected agency staff, should write the rules people live under, and Congress has used broad delegations to avoid accountability. But its remedy is drastic — a near-total halt to federal rulemaking, since Congress demonstrably cannot write technical rules itself. The practical result would be fewer enforceable rules for everyone, which in practice benefits regulated businesses more than anyone else. The accountability goal and the deregulation effect are inseparable in this design.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Paul introduced it and the Senate sent it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never considered it; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the bill on June 4, 2020 [S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day [S5].
No senator joined as a cosponsor — the cosponsor count was zero [S4].
No further action was taken after the referral: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing regulatory system stayed intact. Federal agencies kept their rulemaking authority, and businesses subject to regulation kept operating under the familiar rules of the status quo — no senator other than the sponsor supported changing that, so nothing was at real risk.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal agencies and the regulatory status quo

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so party splits were never recorded; support did not fall along party lines — a lone Republican sponsor drew zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.industry: Regulated businesses (manufacturers, energy producers, financial firms, drug and food companies)
industries.note: The bill would strip agencies of the power to issue or update rules unless Congress wrote every detail into statute, leaving industries with far fewer enforceable federal rules. The gain to these industries comes at the cost of the protections ordinary people get from those rules.

The bill would end the core function of agencies like EPA, FDA, and OSHA — turning broad statutory mandates into specific rules — by voiding any rule not fully defined in an act of Congress. Agency power protects the public in many areas but also embodies the unelected-lawmaking problem the bill targets, so its interest cuts both ways.

The bill creates a new cause of action letting anyone sue to block enforcement of any rule not fully defined in statute, opening a large new field of federal lawsuits. Whether that serves the public depends on the case.
